title: Tangkhul Folk Riddles (Tungtuktui): Metaphorical Cognition and Oral Pedagogy
alternate_titles: Cognitive Structure, Enigmas, and Linguistic Play in Tangkhul Riddles
journal: Folklore & Oral Traditions of Northeast India
publisher: Tribal Research Institute & ICSSR, New Delhi
subject: Folklore, Oral Riddles & Cognitive Linguistics
notes: Structural and cognitive analysis of 400 Tangkhul folk riddles (Tungtuktui), demonstrating metaphor mapping and oral intellectual games.
abstract: Tungtuktui (folk riddles) constitute one of the most vibrant intellectual pastimes of traditional Tangkhul evening gatherings in village dormitories and family hearths. This paper investigates the cognitive structures, metaphor mappings, and pedagogical functions of Tangkhul riddling. We analyze 400 collected riddles across four semantic domains: human anatomy, household implements, flora/fauna, and celestial phenomena, demonstrating how riddles cultivate rapid analogical reasoning in youth.

sections.content: A riddling session opens with the ritual formula: 'Tungtuk-tui akha hang-sa!' (Let me cast a riddle!). The audience responds in unison: 'Rarlu, ithumna pamsaye!' (Bring it forth, we are ready!). The challenger poses the metaphoric enigma, and the participants offer competing guesses until the correct solution is hailed.

sections.title: 2. Structural Typology: Animal and Anatomy Metaphors
sections.content: Tangkhul riddles rely on vivid domestic comparisons. For instance, the traditional carrying basket (Phurwon) is personified as a woman who eats firewood and carries stones; teeth are thirty-two white warriors standing guard in a crimson cave; and rain is a thousand silver needles sewing sky to mountain.

sections.title: 3. Pedagogical and Social Cognitive Value
sections.content: Beyond recreation, Tungtuktui served as oral encyclopedias. Children learned animal tracking habits, forest plant traits, and linguistic vocabulary by deciphering these poetic enigmas during winter evenings beside the glowing hearth.
